sources.title: Phương pháp chữa bệnh thối vây ở cá (Mytour)
Fin Rot in Pet Fish (Dr. Jessie Sanders, Aquatic Veterinary Services)
5 Quick and Easy Steps for Treating Fin Rot (Aquarium Co-Op)

facts.fact: An aquatic vet describes fin rot as an active infection of the fins that can spread to other skin and sometimes becomes systemic.
Fin rot is a bacterial disease that leaves fins and tail ragged or discolored, and it is common in bettas and goldfish.
The decay starts at the fin edge and moves inward. Once it reaches the fin base, the lost tissue cannot regrow.
Untreated fin rot can spread to the body as fin-and-body rot and kill the fish.
Mortality can come within days and rises sharply once bacteria reach the bloodstream.
In mild cases, the soft fin-ray tissue can grow back fully once the infection is cleared.
Long, delicate fins, such as those of bettas and fancy goldfish, are awkward to use and get injured often.
Stage 1 is discoloration at the fin edges, which can look white, red or black depending on the fish's color.
Stage 2 is frayed, uneven edges as dead tissue falls away. Stage 3 is loss of the whole fin or tail, with the infection spreading to the body.
Fin rot often starts with red streaks in the fins, then the fin edges turn abnormally pale, then the membrane frays or rots.
Early signs include frayed edges, a reddened tail fin and greyish fin tips. Advanced cases erode and bleed back to the caudal peduncle and can expose the skeleton.
Affected fish may stop eating, become lethargic and turn darker.
Bacterial fin rot leaves a whitish-grey edge and patchy damage. Fungal fin rot looks creamy-white and hairy, with more even damage.
Bacterial (Pseudomonas) rot frays the fin raggedly. Fungal rot erodes more evenly and more often leaves a white edge.
A healing wound often regrows white or translucent tissue, and clear or white regrowth at the tail is normal. Red tissue means infection is still active.
Fish with naturally uneven fin edges, such as halfmoon bettas, can make fin rot hard to spot.
Regrown fins may come back in a different color.
A sure diagnosis needs a necropsy plus bacterial culture and isolation.
The usual bacteria are Aeromonas, Pseudomonas and Flavobacterium, which often live normally in the fish's skin mucus.
LiveAquaria names Aeromonas, Pseudomonas and Flexibacter as the cause. These bacteria are normally in the water and only cause disease when fish are weakened.
In a 2004 study, Aeromonas hydrophila was the most common isolate (198 of 468) and was highly virulent, followed by Pseudomonas fluorescens (102) and Flavobacterium columnare (36).
Bacterial and fungal infections can occur together.
Fin rot usually starts as a wound that becomes infected. Fin tissue has little blood supply, so infection can spread locally.
Predisposing factors include poor water quality, injury, poor diet and stress. Fin rot can also be secondary to another disease.
Aggressive encounters that damage fins often lead to secondary bacterial or fungal infection.
Named stressors include dirty water, fin nipping, an overly strong filter, sharp decor, wrong temperature, overcrowding and overfeeding.
Mytour names tetras, serpae tetras, black skirt tetras, angelfish and catfish as fin nippers that should be kept away from vulnerable fish such as guppies.
Even soft plant roots and unsuitable decor can snag long fins and cause the first wound.
Test the water at once and look for stressors, then remove the stressor right away.
Isolate the sick fish in a separate tank of clean, dechlorinated water, and use a separate net for each tank.
If an infected area is red, check water chemistry, environment and diet. If all are fine, contact an aquatic vet.
Remove fin-nipping or fighting fish and correct water problems to stop the rot from coming back.
An aquatic vet says improving the environment (water quality, diet, conditions that support immunity) is the best treatment for fin rot.
The same vet says antibiotics are rarely recommended for fin rot because they are hard to deliver to the fin tips.
The same vet advises against water-column medications for simple fin rot because they disrupt the biological filter.
Persistent infections may need a vet for antibiotic injections and cleaning or trimming of the affected tissue.
Aquarium Co-Op recommends erythromycin for fin rot and methylene blue if a secondary fungal infection is present.
Aquarium Co-Op says aquarium salt can be used if erythromycin is unavailable but generally works more slowly. It gives no salt dose.
Medication may take several days to work. Recovery signs are that the rot stops spreading, appetite returns and fins begin to regrow.
Routine salt at 1–3 g/L is tolerated by most tropical fish and is safe for the biological filter.
Salt-tolerant species can take a 20–30 minute bath at 10 g/L.
Adult rainbowfish tolerate up to 17 g/L salt and juveniles up to 12 g/L.
Kanamycin can be given in food at 200–300 mg per 100 g of food.
A kanamycin bath of 2–5 g/L for 4–5 days, followed by a 35–50% water change, is listed.
Water-soluble nalidixic acid can be used as a 13 mg/L bath for 1–4 hours, repeated if needed.
Malachite green at 1–3 mg/L for up to 1 hour is effective in some cases.
ANGFA advises thinking carefully before using antibiotics and following the maker's directions for commercial products, since concentrations vary.
Other listed options are salt baths for species that tolerate salt, gentian violet dabbed on the lesion, and antibiotics in a treatment tank.
Seachem KanaPlex (kanamycin) lists fin rot with a treatment period of 7 days or until the infection clears.
KanaPlex water dose: 1 measure per 20 L (5 gallons), repeated every 48 hours, for a maximum of 3 doses.
Seachem says a second back-to-back KanaPlex round is possible for severe cases, but only if fish show no stress at the end of the first round.
Seachem says to remove all invertebrates (shrimp, snails) before dosing KanaPlex in the water, because they are extremely sensitive to medication.
KanaPlex can be fed instead (1 scoop KanaPlex, 1 scoop Focus, 1 tbsp food, daily for up to 1 week), and Seachem calls this medicated food excellent for tanks with invertebrates.
Seachem says to turn off UV and ozone and remove carbon or Purigen while dosing KanaPlex, then remove it afterward with activated carbon. It does not harm the filter bed.
Mytour lists antibacterials containing erythromycin, minocycline, trimethoprim or sulfadimidine. It says to choose dye-free products and use them for the period on the label.
Mytour advises medicating only if the fish does not improve after a few days of cleaning and water correction.
Mytour suggests keeping the water at 26–27°C and pH 7–8 during treatment.
Mytour gives a salt dose of 30 g per 4 L, only for salt-tolerant freshwater fish. This is far above ANGFA's routine 1–3 g/L.
Medications reduce dissolved oxygen, so add an air stone or sponge filter during treatment.
Mytour says that for bettas the aeration should be kept low so the current does not stress the fish.
Step 1: test water parameters and look for stressors such as a strong current, sharp decor, wrong temperature or nippers.
Step 2: remove the stressor right away.
Step 3: clean the tank and remove as much waste as possible, since many medications require skipping water changes during treatment.
Step 4: medicate if needed, for example erythromycin, or methylene blue for secondary fungus.
Step 5: keep conditions comfortable and add aeration while medicating.
Mytour says unfiltered tanks can have a 100% water change with dechlorinated water. Tanks with an established biological filter should have only about 50% changed.
Rinse filter media in tank water, not tap water.
Keep water quality excellent, avoid fin injuries, reduce stress and remove dead or sick fish promptly.
Never add sick fish to a community tank. Quarantine or treat them first.
Clean the tank on a schedule, avoid overstocking and overfeeding, and add live plants to absorb waste.
Use a heater to hold the right temperature, slow strong currents and remove aggressive tankmates.
Check the fish every day, ideally at feeding time, to catch early signs.
Trim plants regularly, use decor suited to long-finned bettas, and give bettas a smooth resting spot.
Mytour suggests changing the water every 3 days in a 4 L tank, every 4–5 days in a 10 L tank and every 7 days in a 20 L tank.
Feed a varied, good-quality diet without overfeeding, since leftovers feed bacteria.
Treating the symptoms without removing the cause, such as nippers, sharp decor or dirty water, lets fin rot come back.
Forgetting to aerate while medicating is a mistake, because medications reduce oxygen.
Mistaking normal white or clear regrowth on a healing fin for active rot is a common error. Only red tissue indicates active infection.
Dosing medication into the water of a tank with shrimp or snails is a mistake. Seachem says to remove invertebrates first or use medicated food.
Routinely mixing medications should be avoided.
Using salt on species that do not tolerate it is a mistake. Check tolerance before a salt bath.
A Vietnamese guide (Mytour) stresses treating tap water with dechlorinator before it goes into the tank or hospital tank.
In Vietnamese, the disease is called bệnh thối vây or thối đuôi. Mytour blames dirty tanks, poor care and contact with sick fish.
Mytour itself says tea tree oil (1–2 drops in the tank) is unproven and should only be used for prevention.
Wikipedia says the belief that pet-store conditions are why bettas commonly get fin rot lacks a citation.
Seachem lists mouth rot (columnaris) among KanaPlex targets and says columnaris is highly contagious, so infected fish should go to a hospital tank.
Fungal secondary infection is common on fin-rot lesions.
